2 Exercise 1

Stamey et al. 1989 examined the correlation between the level of prostate-specific antigen (PSA) and a number of clinical measures in men who were about to receive a radical prostatectomy. PSA is a protein that is produced by the prostate gland. The higher a man’s PSA level, the more likely it is that he has prostate cancer.  Use the prostate cancer dataset, described here, to train a model that predicts log of prostate-specific antigen. The variables are

- log cancer volume (lcavol)
- log prostate weight (lweight)
- age
- log of the amount of benign prostatic hyperplasia (lbph)
- seminal vesicle invasion (svi)
- log of capsular penetration (lcp)
- Gleason score (gleason)
- percent of Gleason scores 4 or 5 (pgg45)

You can ignore column named “train” and do your own data splitting. Do not forget to perform feature selection!
You can use as examples the Linear Regression Lab and the section related to feature selection from Lab: Linear Models and Regularization Methods from the book An Introduction to Statistical Learning.

2.1 Data preparation & Splitting

Before splitting the dataset into training and testing sets, an exploratory data analysis was conducted to examine feature relationships and detect potential multicollinearity issues. The analysis revealed some correlations between variables, particularly when comparing categorical vs. numerical features. However, since all Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) values remain below 5, indicating an acceptable level of multicollinearity, no variables were removed from the model.

### Load dataset
prostate_data <- read.delim("data/prostate_data.txt")
prostate_data <- prostate_data %>% column_to_rownames(var = "X")

# Drop the "train" column
prostate_data <- prostate_data[, !colnames(prostate_data) %in% "train"]

# Identify categorical and numercial variables
categorical_vars <- c("svi", "gleason")
numerical_vars <- setdiff(colnames(prostate_data), c(categorical_vars, "lpsa"))

# Convert categorical variables to factors
prostate_data <- prostate_data %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(categorical_vars), as.factor))

### Exploratory Data Analysis Before Splitting

## Boxplots for numerical vs categorical comparisons

# svi vs. numerical variables

par(mfrow = c(2, 3)) 

svi_colors <- c("No" = "#F8766D", "Yes" = "#00BFC4")  

for (num_var in numerical_vars) {
  test <- t.test(prostate_data[[num_var]] ~ prostate_data$svi)
  p_val <- test$p.value
  
  p_label <- ifelse(p_val < 0.001, "p-value < 0.001", paste("p-value =", round(p_val, 3)))
  
  svi_factor <- factor(prostate_data$svi, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes"))
  
  boxplot(prostate_data[[num_var]] ~ svi_factor, 
          main = paste(num_var, "by svi\n", p_label),
          xlab = "svi", ylab = num_var, 
          col = svi_colors, border = "black")
}

# gleason vs. numerical variables
par(mfrow = c(2, 3)) 

gleason_colors <- c("6" = "#F8766D", 
                    "7" = "#7CAE00",  
                    "8" = "#00BFC4", 
                    "9" = "#C77CFF") 

for (num_var in numerical_vars) {
  anova_model <- aov(prostate_data[[num_var]] ~ prostate_data$gleason)
  anova_summary <- summary(anova_model)[[1]]
  p_val <- anova_summary["Pr(>F)"][1,]
  
  p_label <- ifelse(p_val < 0.001, "p-value < 0.001", paste("p-value =", round(p_val, 3)))
  
  gleason_factor <- factor(prostate_data$gleason, levels = c(6, 7, 8, 9))
  
  boxplot(prostate_data[[num_var]] ~ gleason_factor, 
          main = paste(num_var, "by gleason\n", p_label),
          xlab = "gleason", ylab = num_var, 
          col = gleason_colors[as.character(levels(gleason_factor))], 
          border = "black")
}

## Correlation matrix to understand numeric variables relationships

cor_matrix <- cor(prostate_data[, numerical_vars], use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

corrplot(
  cor_matrix, 
  method = "color", 
  col = colorRampPalette(c("#bc5090", "white", "#6b85d8"))(200),  
  tl.col = "black",      
  tl.srt = 30,           
  addCoef.col = "black", 
  cl.pos = "b",          
  title = "    Correlation Matrix", 
  mar = c(2, 2, 4, 2),   
  tl.cex = 1.2,          
  number.cex = 0.9       
)

## Relationship between categorical variables

# Create contingency table
svi_gleason_table <- table(prostate_data$svi, prostate_data$gleason)

# Perform Chi-Square Test
chisq_test <- chisq.test(svi_gleason_table)
chisq_stat <- round(chisq_test$statistic, 3)  # Round Chi-squared statistic
p_val <- chisq_test$p.value
p_label <- ifelse(p_val < 0.001, "p-value < 0.001", paste("p-value =", round(p_val, 3)))

# Compute Cramér's V
cramer_v_value <- CramerV(svi_gleason_table)

# Convert the contingency table into a data frame
svi_gleason_df <- as.data.frame(as.table(svi_gleason_table))
colnames(svi_gleason_df) <- c("svi", "gleason", "count")

# Convert categorical variables to factors
svi_gleason_df$svi <- factor(svi_gleason_df$svi, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes"))
svi_gleason_df$gleason <- factor(svi_gleason_df$gleason, levels = c(6, 7, 8, 9))

plot_title <- paste0(
  "Association Between SVI and Gleason Score\n",
  "Cramér's V = ", round(cramer_v_value, 3), 
  " | Chi-sq = ", chisq_stat, " | ", p_label
)

ggplot(svi_gleason_df, aes(x = gleason, y = svi, fill = count)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = count), color = "black", size = 6) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#bc5090", high = "#6b85d8") +
  labs(title = plot_title, x = "Gleason Score", y = "SVI") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) 

# Check Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) for multicollinearity
vif_values <- vif(lm(lpsa ~ ., data = prostate_data))

vif_df <- as.data.frame(vif_values)
vif_df$Feature <- rownames(vif_df)  
vif_df <- vif_df[, c("Feature", "GVIF")]  
colnames(vif_df) <- c("Variable", "VIF")  

# Round VIF values for better readability
vif_df$VIF <- round(vif_df$VIF, 3)

# Transpose the table for a better layout
vif_transposed <- as.data.frame(t(vif_df[, 2, drop = FALSE])) 
colnames(vif_transposed) <- vif_df$Variable  
rownames(vif_transposed) <- "VIF"  # Rename row to "VIF"

# Create a grob table
vif_table <- tableGrob(vif_transposed, rows = NULL)

# Title
vif_title <- textGrob("Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)", 
                      gp = gpar(fontsize = 14, fontface = "bold"))

# Arrange table in a plot
grid.arrange(vif_title, vif_table, nrow = 2)

### Split data
set.seed(42) 

prostate_data_split <- initial_split(prostate_data, prop = 0.7, strata = lpsa) 
train_data <- training(prostate_data_split)
test_data <- testing(prostate_data_split)

# Standardize numerical features
preProcess_model <- preProcess(train_data %>% dplyr::select(-svi, -gleason, -lpsa), 
                               method = c("center", "scale"))

features_train_scaled <- predict(preProcess_model, train_data %>% dplyr::select(-svi, -gleason, -lpsa)) %>%
  bind_cols(train_data %>% dplyr::select(svi, gleason))

features_test_scaled <- predict(preProcess_model, test_data %>% dplyr::select(-svi, -gleason, -lpsa)) %>%
  bind_cols(test_data %>% dplyr::select(svi, gleason))

target_train <- train_data$lpsa
target_test <- test_data$lpsa

2.2 Feature Selection

Lasso regression was used to perform feature selection ensuring that only the most relevant predictors are retained while reducing the risk of overfitting.

# LASSO Feature Selection
set.seed(42)
lasso_cv <- cv.glmnet(as.matrix(features_train_scaled), target_train, alpha = 1, nfolds = 10)
best_lambda <- lasso_cv$lambda.1se

lasso_model <- glmnet(as.matrix(features_train_scaled), target_train, alpha = 1, lambda = best_lambda)
selected_features_lasso <- rownames(coef(lasso_model))[coef(lasso_model)[,1] != 0]
selected_features_lasso <- setdiff(selected_features_lasso, "(Intercept)")  

cat("Selected Features:\n", paste(selected_features_lasso, collapse = ", "), "\n")
## Selected Features:
##  lcavol, lweight, svi

2.3 Model Building

A multiple linear regression model is trained using the features selected by LASSO regression. The model is then used to predict the logarithm of PSA levels in the test dataset.

# Train a linear regression model with selected features
set.seed(42)
features_train_selected <- features_train_scaled[, selected_features_lasso]
features_test_selected <- features_test_scaled[, selected_features_lasso]

lm_model <- lm(lpsa ~ ., data = data.frame(lpsa = target_train, features_train_selected))

2.4 Model Evaluation

The model is evaluated using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), and Coefficient of Determination (R²). Additionally, a scatter plot is generated to compare actual versus predicted values.

#Predict on test data
target_pred <- predict(lm_model, newdata = as.data.frame(features_test_selected))

# Evaluate model performance
mse <- mean((target_test - target_pred)^2)
rmse <- sqrt(mse)
r2 <- summary(lm(target_test ~ target_pred))$r.squared

plot_data <- data.frame(Actual = target_test, Predicted = target_pred)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = Actual, y = Predicted)) +
  geom_point(color = "#6b85d8") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#6b85d8", fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Actual vs Predicted lpsa",
    x = "Actual lpsa",
    y = "Predicted lpsa"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0.5),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    panel.border = element_blank(),
    axis.line = element_line(color = "black", linewidth = 0.5),
    axis.ticks = element_line(color = "black", linewidth = 0.5)
  ) +
  annotate("text", 
           x = min(plot_data$Actual) + 0.5, 
           y = max(plot_data$Predicted) - 0.5, 
           label = sprintf("R² = %.3f\nRMSE = %.3f", r2, rmse),  
           size = 5, color = "black", fontface = "bold")

The R² for the model predicting log PSA levels is 0.732, indicating that 73.2% of the variance in the dependent variable (lpsa) is explained by the selected predictors. This suggests a strong relationship between the independent variables and the response, supporting the model’s effectiveness in capturing key factors influencing PSA levels. Given that biological data often exhibit inherent variability due to unobserved genetic and environmental influences, an R² of 0.732 is considered highly acceptable in this context. Additionally, feature selection via LASSO regression ensured that only the most relevant predictors were retained, reducing overfitting and enhancing model interpretability. The RMSE of 0.587 further supports the model’s predictive accuracy by demonstrating a reasonable deviation between actual and predicted values.

3 Exercise 2

Use the breast cancer dataset to train a model that predicts whether a future tumor image (with unknown diagnosis) is a benign or malignant tumor. Try different machine learning algorithms such as: 

- KNNs
- Decision trees
- Random forest - Logistic Regression

The breast cancer dataset contains digitized breast cancer image features, and was created by Dr. William H. Wolberg, W. Nick Street, and Olvi L. Mangasarian. Each row in the data set represents an image of a tumor sample, including the diagnosis (benign or malignant) and several other measurements (nucleus texture, perimeter, area, and more). Diagnosis for each image was conducted by physicians.

Do not forget to perform hyperparameter tuning!
Generate a ROC curve for all the models.

You can use as a guide the analysis of this dataset included in the chapter 5 of the Data Science, A First Introduction Book. Additionally, for further information and ideas, you can check this post

3.1 ML analysis

In order to train a model that predicts whether a future tumor image is benign or malignant, we will train four different ML algorithms using the Breast Cancer Data set by using the tidymodels framework.

As a first step, we will split the data set into training (80%) and testing (20%) subsets. Then, we will create a 5-fold cross-validation split from our training data, by using the vfold_cv() function.

Next, we will define a single workflow to train the models, perform hyperparameter tuning, and evaluate their performance. This workflow will be applied to each model with its respective grid of tuning parameters, taking into account the dataset size and complexity.

Finally, we will compare the models’ performance using a ROC curve to determine which algorithm performs the best for this data set.

3.1.1 Data preparation & splitting

data <- read.csv("data/breast_cancer_data.csv", row.names = 1)
data$X <- NULL
data <- data %>% mutate(diagnosis = factor(diagnosis, levels = c("B", "M")))

set.seed(42)
data_split <- initial_split(data, prop = 0.8, strata = diagnosis)
bc_train <- training(data_split)
bc_test <- testing(data_split)

set.seed(42)
cv_folds <- vfold_cv(bc_train, v = 5, strata = diagnosis)

3.1.2 Recipe and pipeline definition

bc_recipe <- recipe(diagnosis ~ ., data = bc_train) %>%
  step_normalize(all_predictors()) %>%
  step_corr(all_predictors(), threshold = 0.9) %>%
  step_nzv(all_predictors())

pipeline <- function(model_spec, grid, model_name) {
  workflow <- workflow() %>% 
    add_recipe(bc_recipe) %>% 
    add_model(model_spec)
  
  ## Hyperparameters Tuning
  tuned_res <- tune_grid(
    workflow,
    resamples = cv_folds,
    grid = grid,
    metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, yardstick::accuracy)
  )
  best_params <- select_best(tuned_res, metric = "accuracy")

  ## Model Refit
  final_model <- finalize_workflow(workflow, best_params)
  final_fit <- last_fit(final_model, data_split)
  
  ## Model Evaluation
  results <- collect_metrics(final_fit)
  predictions <- collect_predictions(final_fit)
  
  conf_mat <- predictions %>%
    conf_mat(truth = diagnosis, estimate = .pred_class)
  
  list(model_name = model_name, results = results, predictions = predictions, confusion_matrix = conf_mat)
}

3.1.3 KNNs

In the KNN model, we use a grid to explores different values for the number of neighbors (k) , testing values from 1 to 100 in increments of 5.

Given that the dataset contains 569 observations and 31 features, this range allows the model to explore both small and large values of k, which balances between overfitting (small k) and underfitting (large k); to find the optimal number of neighbors.

knn_spec <- nearest_neighbor(mode = "classification", neighbors = tune()) %>% 
  set_engine("kknn")
knn_grid <- tibble(neighbors = seq(from = 1, to = 100, by = 5))

set.seed(42)
knn_results <- pipeline(knn_spec, knn_grid, "KNN")
fourfoldplot(knn_results$confusion_matrix$table, color=c("#e0938d","#9ed7ab"))

3.1.4 Decision tree

In the Decision Tree model, we use a grid to optimize the minimum number of observations required to split a node (min_n) and the maximum tree depth (tree_depth).

The range of min_n from 2 to 50 and of tree_depth from 1 to 10 ensures that the tree can adjust to different levels of detail.

rpart_spec <- decision_tree(min_n = tune(), tree_depth = tune()) %>%
  set_engine("rpart") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

rpart_grid <- grid_regular(min_n(range = c(2, 50)), tree_depth(range = c(1, 10)), levels = 10)

set.seed(42)
rpart_results <- pipeline(rpart_spec, rpart_grid, "Decision Tree")
fourfoldplot(rpart_results$confusion_matrix$table, color=c("#e0938d","#9ed7ab"))

3.1.5 Random forest

In the Random Forest model, the grid searches for an optimal ensemble size with trees ranging from 500 to 5000. The mtry range (1 to 19) allows for exploring different levels of randomness in feature selection for each split. And the min_n range from 2 to 20 helps control the size of each tree, with larger values preventing overly deep trees and thus reducing overfitting.

rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = tune(), mtry = tune(), min_n = tune()) %>%
  set_engine("ranger", replace = FALSE) %>%
  set_mode("classification")

rf_grid <- grid_regular(trees(range = c(500, 5000)), mtry(range = c(1, 19)), min_n(range = c(2, 20)), levels = 4)

set.seed(42)
rf_results <- pipeline(rf_spec, rf_grid, "Random Forest")
fourfoldplot(rf_results$confusion_matrix$table, color=c("#e0938d","#9ed7ab"))

3.1.6 Logistic regression

Finally, in the Logistic Regression model, with 569 observations and 31 features, regularization is crucial to prevent overfitting, especially for GLMs. The penalty range from 0 to 1 explores no regularization (0) to full regularization (1). The mixture range allows testing a mix between Lasso (L1 regularization) and Ridge (L2 regularization), with values from 0 (Ridge) to 1 (Lasso), to find the best regularization technique for the dataset.

glm_spec <- logistic_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = tune()) %>%
  set_engine("glmnet") %>%
  set_mode("classification")
glm_grid <- grid_regular(penalty(range = c(0, 1)), mixture(range = c(0, 1)), levels = 10)

set.seed(42)
glm_results <- pipeline(glm_spec, glm_grid, "Logistic Regression")
fourfoldplot(glm_results$confusion_matrix$table, color=c("#e0938d","#9ed7ab"))

3.2 Results

3.2.1 ROC curves plot

roc_data <- bind_rows(
  knn_results$predictions %>% 
    mutate(Model = paste0("KNN (AUC: ", round(knn_results$results %>%
    filter(.metric == "roc_auc") %>% pull(.estimate), 3), ")")),
  rpart_results$predictions %>% 
    mutate(Model = paste0("Decision tree (AUC: ", round(rpart_results$results %>%
    filter(.metric == "roc_auc") %>% pull(.estimate), 3), ")")),
  rf_results$predictions %>%
    mutate(Model = paste0("Random forest (AUC: ", round(rf_results$results %>% 
    filter(.metric == "roc_auc") %>% pull(.estimate), 3), ")")),
  glm_results$predictions %>%
    mutate(Model = paste0("Logistic regression (AUC: ", round(glm_results$results %>%
    filter(.metric == "roc_auc") %>% pull(.estimate), 3), ")")))

roc_data %>%
  mutate(diagnosis = factor(diagnosis, levels = c("B", "M"))) %>%
  group_by(Model) %>%
  roc_curve(truth = diagnosis, .pred_M, event_level = "second") %>%
  autoplot() + 
  style_roc() +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = "gray")

3.2.2 Accuracy vs ROC

Model Accuracy AUC
KNN 0.9478261 0.9657623
Decision Tree 0.9478261 0.9286176
Random Forest 0.9304348 0.9886951
Logistic Regression 0.8608696 0.9673773

3.3 Discussion

Which of all models performs better for this data? Discuss.

Overall, all models show strong performance. While Random Forest achieves the highest AUC (0.988), KNN and Decision Tree models have the higher accuracy, due to its lower FP and FN fractions.

Accuracy is highly dependent on the decision threshold used for classification, whereas AUC provides a better assessment of a model’s ability to discriminate between classes across multiple thresholds. So, a model with lower FP and FN at a single threshold may achieve higher accuracy but might not necessarily have the best overall classification ability.

  • KNN and Decision Tree models may be making more conservative predictions, reducing misclassifications at a fixed threshold. However, this does not ensure generalization across different thresholds, which could explain their lower AUC.

  • In contrast, Random Forest benefits from increased robustness and classification performance across different thresholds. Although it may produce more FP or FN at a specific threshold, its ability to rank positive instances higher than negative ones contributes to its higher AUC performance.

Taking into account that in this analysis model performance was assessed using the default threshold, we can conclude that based on the ROC metric the best-performing model for this data set is Random Forest.

4 Exercise 3

Use The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) gene expression data of two different cancer types to build a machine learning model that identifies whether a given sample (gene counts) belongs to one or the other. The TCGA is a comprehensive and coordinated effort to accelerate our understanding of the molecular basis of cancer through the application of genome analysis technologies, including large-scale genome sequencing. The program has generated, analyzed, and made available genomic sequence, expression, methylation, and copy number variation data on over 11,000 individuals who represent over 30 different types of cancer. After building your model, you should predict the cancer types for 10 unkwnon samples.

For this task, you should retrieve the TCGA data from the Genomic Data Commons Data Portal. If necessary you can watch the video uploaded in the Campus Global. The video assumes that you have previously installed the GDC data transfer tool.

Each team will work with two specific cancer types, that will be assigned in class.

Important notice: if you do not have a lot of hard drive space in your laptop, you can modify the manifest file to download only 50 samples per cancer types.

4.1 Data preparation

This section focuses on data preparation by retrieving and structuring gene expression data from TCGA for two cancer types: LAML and KIRC. The prepare_data() function systematically loads gene expression files, extracts relevant data, and removes unnecessary metadata. Each sample is assigned a unique identifier, and gene expression values are averaged to ensure consistency. The processed data from both cancer types is then merged into a single dataset, aligning gene names and expression values across samples. For this analysis, we use the TPM values of each sample, as this measure is the most suitable for RNA-seq comparisons between samples.

prepare_data <- function(tcga_path, start_index = 1) {
  folders <- list.dirs(tcga_path, recursive = FALSE)
  files_list <- lapply(folders, function(folder) {
    list.files(folder, pattern = "gene_counts.tsv$", recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)
  })

  merged_df <- NULL
  for (i in seq_along(files_list)) {
    df <- as.data.frame(read_tsv(files_list[[i]], comment = "#", col_names = TRUE, show_col_types = FALSE))
    df <- df[-c(1, 2, 3, 4), ]
    df <- df[, c("gene_name", "tpm_unstranded")]
    
    colnames(df) <- c("gene_name", paste0("sample", start_index + i))  # Adjust sample names
    
    df <- df %>%
      group_by(gene_name) %>%
      summarise(across(where(is.numeric), ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)), .groups = "drop")

    if (is.null(merged_df)) {
      merged_df <- df
    } else {
      merged_df <- full_join(merged_df, df, by = "gene_name")
    }
  }
  return(merged_df)
}

laml_data <- prepare_data("data/TCGA/LAML", start_index = 1)   
kirc_data <- prepare_data("data/TCGA/KIRC", start_index = 152)  
merged_data <- full_join(laml_data, kirc_data, by = "gene_name")

data <- as.data.frame(t(merged_data[,-1]))  
colnames(data) <- merged_data$gene_name     
dim(data)
## [1]   300 59427
data$type <- rep(c("LAML", "KIRC"), times = c(150, 150))
data <- data %>%
  relocate(type)

4.2 Data Splitting and Feature Selection

The dataset is split into training (70%) and testing (30%) sets. To enhance model performance, feature selection is applied by calculating the variance of each gene’s expression within the training set, as genes with higher variance are more likely to carry discriminative information. The top 25 genes with the highest variance are selected, reducing dimensionality while preserving relevant features. Finally, 10-fold cross-validation is established, allowing for robust model evaluation by iteratively training and testing on different data subsets, thereby reducing overfitting and improving generalizability.

set.seed(42)
data_split <- initial_split(data, prop = 0.7, strata = type)
tcga_train <- training(data_split)
tcga_test <- testing(data_split)


gene_variances <- apply(tcga_train[, -1], 2, var, na.rm = TRUE)

# Select the top 25 genes with the highest variance
selected_genes <- names(sort(gene_variances, decreasing = TRUE))[1:25]

# Keep only selected genes in both train and test sets
tcga_train <- tcga_train %>%
  dplyr::select(type, all_of(selected_genes))

tcga_test <- tcga_test %>%
  dplyr::select(type, all_of(selected_genes))

set.seed(42)
cv_folds <- vfold_cv(tcga_train, v = 10, strata = type)

4.3 Recipe and pipeline definition

The tcga_recipe applies, first, normalization to scale all features to ensure they are on a comparable scale. Then, highly correlated features are removed, preventing redundancy and multicollinearity. Near-zero variance filtering eliminates genes that show little variation across samples, as they contribute minimally to classification. Finally, PCA is applied to reduce dimensionality while retaining 90% of the variance, improving efficiency and reducing overfitting risks. The pipeline() function integrates this preprocessing with any model, performing hyperparameter tuning, model selection, and evaluation using cross-validation. It identifies the best parameters, refits the model, and collects performance metrics.

tcga_recipe <- recipe(type ~ ., data = tcga_train) %>%
  step_normalize(all_predictors()) %>%
  step_corr(all_predictors(), threshold = 0.8) %>%
  step_nzv(all_predictors(), freq_cut = 95/5, unique_cut = 10) %>%  
  step_pca(all_predictors(), threshold = 0.9)


pipeline <- function(model_spec, grid, model_name) {
  workflow <- workflow() %>% 
    add_recipe(tcga_recipe) %>% 
    add_model(model_spec)
  
  ## Hyperparameters Tuning
  tuned_res <- tune_grid(
    workflow,
    resamples = cv_folds,
    grid = grid,
    metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, yardstick::accuracy)
  )
  best_params <- select_best(tuned_res, metric = "accuracy")

  ## Model Refit
  final_model <- finalize_workflow(workflow, best_params)
  final_fit <- last_fit(final_model, data_split)
  
  ## Model Evaluation
  results <- collect_metrics(final_fit)
  predictions <- collect_predictions(final_fit)
  
  conf_mat <- predictions %>%
    conf_mat(truth = type, estimate = .pred_class)
  
  list(model_name = model_name, results = results, predictions = predictions, confusion_matrix = conf_mat, final_model = final_fit)
}

4.4 Random forest

We decided to build a Random Forest model, as it have been widely used and perform well on gene expression datasets. It also works well with high-dimensional data and handles non-linearity and interactions between genes.

The Random Forest classifier is used for cancer type prediction, with hyperparameters optimized through grid search to balance performance, generalization, and efficiency. The number of trees (50–300) ensures stability without excessive computation, while limiting the number of features per split (1–3) helps prevent overfitting, given the small gene set. A minimum node size of 50–150 prevents overly deep splits that could capture noise rather than meaningful patterns. Using 80% of the data per tree introduces randomness, improving generalization. The ranger engine was chosen for its speed and built-in feature importance metrics, ensuring the model remains accurate, interpretable, and robust for predicting unseen cancer samples.

rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = tune(), mtry = tune(), min_n = tune()) %>%
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity", replace = FALSE, sample.fraction = 0.8) %>%
  set_mode("classification")

rf_grid <- grid_regular(
  trees(range = c(50, 300)),  
  mtry(range = c(1, 3)),      
  min_n(range = c(50, 150)),
  levels = 4
)

set.seed(42)
rf_results <- pipeline(rf_spec, rf_grid, "Random Forest")
fourfoldplot(rf_results$confusion_matrix$table, color=c("#e0938d","#9ed7ab"))

The Random Forest model performs exceptionally well in distinguishing LAML and KIRC cancer types, with a very low error rate.

4.5 Logistic regression

As a second model, Logistic Regression is a good option, particularly because it is well-suited for binary classification, which is the type of problem we are dealing with.

The Logistic Regression classifier is implemented for cancer type prediction. The penalty term (0.01–10, log-scaled) controls the strength of regularization, preventing overfitting while maintaining predictive accuracy. The elastic net mixing parameter (0–1) determines the balance between L1 (lasso) and L2 (ridge) regularization, enabling both feature selection and coefficient shrinkage. A more granular grid search (10 levels) ensures optimal tuning of these hyperparameters. The glmnet engine was chosen for its computational efficiency and ability to handle high-dimensional gene expression data, making it well-suited for this classification task.

glm_spec <- logistic_reg(
  penalty = tune(),  
  mixture = tune()   
) %>%
  set_engine("glmnet") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

glm_grid <- grid_regular(
  penalty(range = c(0.01, 10), trans = log10_trans()),  
  mixture(range = c(0, 1)), 
  levels = 10  
)

set.seed(42)
glm_results <- pipeline(glm_spec, glm_grid, "Logistic Regression")
fourfoldplot(glm_results$confusion_matrix$table, color=c("#e0938d","#9ed7ab"))

The Logistic Regression model performs exceptionally well in distinguishing LAML and KIRC cancer types, with a very low error rate.

4.6 ROC curves

ROC curves and AUC scores were used to evaluate the classification performance of the Logistic Regression and Random Forest models. Both models, Logistic Regression (AUC: 0.988) and Random Forest (AUC: 0.976), demonstrate excellent discrimination.

roc_data <- bind_rows(
  rf_results$predictions %>%
    mutate(Model = paste0("Random Forest (AUC: ", round(rf_results$results %>%
    filter(.metric == "roc_auc") %>% pull(.estimate), 3), ")")),
  glm_results$predictions %>%
    mutate(Model = paste0("Logistic Regression (AUC: ", round(glm_results$results %>%
    filter(.metric == "roc_auc") %>% pull(.estimate), 3), ")"))
)

roc_data %>%
  mutate(type = factor(type, levels = c("LAML", "KIRC"))) %>%
  group_by(Model) %>%
  roc_curve(truth = type, .pred_KIRC, event_level = "second") %>%
  autoplot() + 
  style_roc() +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = "gray")

4.7 Predict Cancer Type for 10 Unlabeled Samples

4.7.1 Prediction using the Logistic Regression Model

This section predicts the cancer type for 10 unknown samples using both the Logistic Regression and Random Forest models, as they achieved similar AUC values (Logistic Regression: 0.988, Random Forest: 0.976). The unknown samples are preprocessed to match the training format, retaining only the selected 25 genes and reshaping the data for prediction. Each model then generates cancer type classifications along with their probability scores for KIRC and LAML. Running both models allows us to validate consistency in predictions, ensuring classification reliability.

# Load unknown samples
unknown_samples <- read_tsv("data/unknwown_samples.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Process the unknown samples
unknown_processed <- unknown_samples %>%
  dplyr::select(gene_name, starts_with("individual_")) %>%
  filter(gene_name %in% selected_genes) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("individual_"), 
               names_to = "sample_id", 
               values_to = "expression") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = gene_name, values_from = expression) %>%
  relocate(sample_id)  

# Extract the fitted model from the workflow
final_workflow <- glm_results$final_model$.workflow[[1]]

# Make predictions
predictions <- predict(final_workflow, new_data = unknown_processed, type = "class")
probabilities <- predict(final_workflow, new_data = unknown_processed, type = "prob")

# Combine results with sample IDs
prediction_results <- bind_cols(
  sample_id = unknown_processed$sample_id,
  predicted_type = predictions$.pred_class,
  probabilities
)

colnames(prediction_results) <- c("Sample ID", "Predicted Cancer Type", "Probability KIRC", "Probability LAML")

results <- prediction_results %>%
  mutate(`Sample ID` = gsub("individual_", "Individual ", `Sample ID`))

kable(results, caption = "Cancer Type Predictions (Using Logsitic Regression Model)", align = "c", "pipe")

4.7.2 Prediction using the Random Forest Model

# Load unknown samples
unknown_samples <- read_tsv("data/unknwown_samples.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Process the unknown samples
unknown_processed <- unknown_samples %>%
  dplyr::select(gene_name, starts_with("individual_")) %>%
  filter(gene_name %in% selected_genes) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("individual_"), 
               names_to = "sample_id", 
               values_to = "expression") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = gene_name, values_from = expression) %>%
  relocate(sample_id)  # Ensure sample_id is the first column

# Extract the fitted model from the workflow
final_workflow <- rf_results$final_model$.workflow[[1]]

# Make predictions
predictions <- predict(final_workflow, new_data = unknown_processed, type = "class")
probabilities <- predict(final_workflow, new_data = unknown_processed, type = "prob")

# Combine results with sample IDs
prediction_results <- bind_cols(
  sample_id = unknown_processed$sample_id,
  predicted_type = predictions$.pred_class,
  probabilities
)

colnames(prediction_results) <- c("Sample ID", "Predicted Cancer Type", "Probability KIRC", "Probability LAML")

results <- prediction_results %>%
  mutate(`Sample ID` = gsub("individual_", "Individual ", `Sample ID`))

kable(results, caption = "Cancer Type Predictions (Using Random Forest Model)", align = "c", "pipe")
Cancer Type Predictions (Using Random Forest Model)
Sample ID Predicted Cancer Type Probability KIRC Probability LAML
Individual 1 KIRC 0.8559632 0.1440368
Individual 2 KIRC 0.7605471 0.2394529
Individual 3 KIRC 0.8815436 0.1184564
Individual 4 KIRC 0.9608882 0.0391118
Individual 5 KIRC 0.8725051 0.1274949
Individual 6 LAML 0.1672489 0.8327511
Individual 7 KIRC 0.7743260 0.2256740
Individual 8 KIRC 0.6640632 0.3359368
Individual 9 KIRC 0.6494777 0.3505223
Individual 10 LAML 0.4966643 0.5033357

The results indicate that both models predict similar outcomes for most individuals in the dataset. Both models classify Individual 6 as belonging to the LAML category, while the remaining individuals are predominantly classified as KIRC. However, a key difference emerges in the case of Individual 10, where the Random Forest model classifies the sample as LAML, whereas Logistic Regression predicts it as KIRC. This inconsistency suggests that the classification of Individual 10 may be ambiguous, requiring further validation through additional data or more refined models. Random Forest produces highly confident predictions, with most probabilities exceeding 0.80, meaning the model is very certain about its classifications. Logistic Regression, in contrast, provides more moderate probability scores, with values closer to 0.50 in several cases, suggesting less confidence in distinguishing between LAML and KIRC. A key limitation of this classification is that the models were trained exclusively on two cancer types, while in reality, there are many more cancer types. This means that the models cannot recognize other potential cancers and must force every sample into one of the two available classes. This explains why some probability values in Logistic Regression are close to 0.50, indicating the model struggles to confidently assign a type. If any of these individuals belong to a different cancer type, the models will still classify them as either KIRC or LAML, even if they are biologically different. Even so, we could speculate that Individual 6 sample is truly from LAML cancer-type based on both ML models classification.
